title: hatDu — Digital Request & Offer Platform
description: Designing a trusted digital platform where verified requesters and providers can connect, manage requests and offers, and collaborate through flexible account roles and permissions.
body:
# hatDu — Digital Request & Offer Platform

A real marketplace product where people post what they need and providers respond with offers. I worked on the product experience across UX/UI, responsive design, product flows and product communication.

## Product snapshot

**Product**  
Digital request-and-offer marketplace

**My role**  
Product Designer · UX/UI · Digital Experience

**Context**  
STG Media Marketing

**Timeline**  
2022–2026

## The product

hatDu connects requesters with providers through a structured request-and-offer workflow. The live product brings together requests, offers, user accounts, verification, permissions and communication in one experience. citeturn0search0

My work sits inside that larger system: understanding how the product should behave, shaping interfaces and flows, and communicating functionality so users can understand what to do next.

![hatDu request and offer platform interface](/images/home_Zeichenfl%C3%A4che%201%20Kopie%2018.jpg "hatDu — Request and Offer Experience")

## The design challenge

### How do you make a complex product feel simple?

hatDu has more complexity than a typical marketing website.

Users can register privately or as a company, participate as requesters or providers, complete verification, manage requests and offers, and work with delegated account access.

That means a decision on one screen can affect the experience somewhere else.

**The goal was not to hide the complexity. It was to structure it so the user understands what matters now and what they can do next.**

## A product decision: one account, multiple roles

One of the product problems I identified was the friction created when a user needed to work in different roles.

The original setup required separate login emails when a person needed to work across requester and provider roles.

I proposed a simpler model:

**One account → switch between requester and provider roles.**

The important design question was not simply how the switch should look. It was how the product should communicate:

- which role is currently active
- which actions belong to that role
- what changes when the role changes
- how the user can stay oriented

This is the kind of product-design problem I enjoy: turning a structural requirement into a clearer interaction model.

## Designing for reuse: Copy & Publish Request

Another contribution was the **Copy & Publish Request** flow.

Instead of recreating a previous request from scratch, a user can reuse an existing request, edit its attributes and publish it again.

The principle is simple:

> **When users repeat a task, the product should help them reuse previous work.**

This reduces repetitive input while keeping the user in control of what is published.

## Trust is part of the experience

A marketplace depends on confidence between people who may not know each other.

hatDu uses identity verification as part of participation. The live platform currently communicates requester trustability and delivery performance directly within request listings. citeturn0search0

That makes verification more than a back-office process.

**It becomes a UX problem.**

The interface needs to explain why verification exists, what the user needs to do, and what changes after verification — without turning the experience into unnecessary friction.

## One account, controlled access

Another layer is delegated account access.

An account can give controlled access to family members or colleagues while the main account owner remains responsible for the account.

That creates a system of relationships:

**Owner → delegated user → permissions → available actions**

The design challenge is to make those relationships understandable without exposing every underlying rule at once.

I approach this by asking:

**What does this person need to understand at this moment?**

That question helps determine what should be visible, what should be explained later and what should remain behind the interaction.

## From product logic to interface

My UI work spans the relationship between:

- information hierarchy
- interaction patterns
- responsive layouts
- typography
- components
- forms
- navigation
- visual consistency

I don't treat each screen as an isolated composition.

I think about how screens behave together as one product — especially when the same user moves between registration, verification, requests, offers and account management.

**Consistency becomes part of usability.**

## Product communication

My role also extends beyond the interface.

For hatDu, I create product demonstrations, motion content, educational material, social content and recorded website walkthroughs.

The live product itself includes tutorials and explanatory material, while the public presence uses visual communication to explain the platform and its value. citeturn0search0turn0search1

This gives me a useful second perspective:

**If a feature is difficult to explain, the product experience and the communication around it both need to become clearer.**

## What I learned

Working on a real product changed how I think about design.

I learned to look beyond the individual screen and consider the system behind it:

**roles → permissions → verification → workflows → states → communication**

A polished interface is only one part of a good product.

The stronger question is:

**Does the product make the right behaviour understandable?**

That is the direction I am taking forward into Product Design.

## My contribution

**Product Design** — shaping product behaviour and interaction models

**UX/UI** — flows, interfaces, responsive layouts and reusable patterns

**Product thinking** — roles, permissions, verification and workflow relationships

**Visual & motion design** — demonstrations, educational content and product communication

**Digital experience** — connecting the product interface with the way the product is explained

## Explore the real product

hatDu is a live product, so this case study can be followed by the actual experience.

**Explore the platform →**

title: Carpooling Mobility Product
description: A route-based carpooling product concept connecting drivers and passengers through GPS-aware journey matching. I designed and developed the UX/UI, interactive journey form, mapping, matching logic, administration tools, data management and Excel reporting.
role: Product Designer · UX/UI · Web App · Mapping · Data
body:
# Carpooling Mobility Product

A digital carpooling concept designed to make everyday journeys more flexible by connecting people already travelling in similar directions.

## The problem

Public transport does not always match people's actual routes, schedules or daily needs. At the same time, many private cars travel the same roads with empty seats.

The concept explores a simple question: **Instead of creating another journey, can an existing journey be shared?**

## The concept

Drivers can offer available seats on journeys they are already making and receive a contribution towards travel costs. Passengers can find practical alternatives to waiting, walking or complicated public-transport connections.

## User experience

I designed the journey-entry experience around collecting enough structured information for meaningful matching while keeping the process understandable. The form captures role, start and destination, via points, dates, times, frequency, days, available seats, child-seat information, preferences, cost contribution and privacy confirmation.

## Interactive route mapping

The product uses Leaflet, Leaflet Routing Machine, OpenStreetMap/Nominatim and OSRM to turn Start → Via → Destination input into visual routes and structured geographic data.

## GPS-based matching

The matching concept considers route overlap alongside direction, travel days, travel times, available seats and journey characteristics. The goal is to identify practical compatibility rather than simply matching people who selected the same area.

## Administration & data

I developed an administration area for reviewing submitted journeys, including permanent journey IDs, journey details, route information, matching information and GPS data. Structured Excel reporting turns submissions into data that can be analysed and presented to organisations or potential partners.

## Product iteration

Testing with real journey submissions revealed an important product-design lesson: high GPS overlap alone does not necessarily mean two journeys are practically compatible. Different destinations, departure times and pickup requirements can still make a match unsuitable. This led to a broader matching model combining **route overlap + direction + time + day + pickup/drop-off compatibility**.

## Technical implementation

The prototype combines responsive HTML/CSS/JavaScript interfaces, interactive mapping, a custom WordPress-based solution, structured journey data, matching logic, administration, permanent IDs and Excel export.

## AI-assisted development

I used AI as a development accelerator while defining the product behaviour, UX, requirements and system logic myself. The project became an iterative cycle of **idea → user problem → UX → prototype → real submissions → data → matching → testing → refinement**.

## What the project demonstrates

**UX/UI Design · Interaction Design · Mapping · Data Design · Matching Logic · Administration · Reporting · Product Thinking · AI-assisted development**
